name: Battle of the Atlantic
question: What changed for a merchant ship crossing the Atlantic in 1943?
objective: Keeping the sea lanes open sustained Britain and made the later build-up of Allied armies possible. The question for each convoy was whether air cover would reach it during the crossing.
turningPoint: In May 1943 long-range shore patrols and escort carriers worked alongside surface groups. Neighbouring convoys had markedly different experiences.
consequence: German submarines continued to sail after the May withdrawal. The Allies could move shipping across the North Atlantic with far greater confidence.
gap: Convoy arrivals, aircraft sightings and submarine attacks have different denominators. An attack report alone cannot establish a sinking.

episodes.title: First HX convoy sails from Halifax
episodes.action: Merchant ships assembled at Halifax for the eastbound passage to Britain. Canadian warships escorted HX 1 on the opening leg.
episodes.outcome: The convoy system became the organising unit for later air and surface protection. Continuous air cover across the ocean was still years away.

episodes.title: ONS 5 survives the night battle
episodes.action: Aircraft operating from Canada supported the passage while much of the fighting fell to the surface escorts beyond dependable shore cover.
episodes.outcome: The convoy suffered merchant losses. The escorts also inflicted losses that made the result costly for the German submarine force.

episodes.place: North Atlantic, HX 237 and SC 129 sector
episodes.title: Aircraft dispatched to HX 237
episodes.action: Coastal Command sent Liberators to escort HX 237. The crews encountered submarines even though they failed to meet the convoy itself.
episodes.outcome: The review distinguished aircraft sent, convoy contact, sightings and attacks. Carrier aircraft also supported these two neighbouring convoys.

episodes.title: SC 130 crosses under air and surface cover
episodes.action: The B7 Escort Group accompanied the Halifax convoy. Coastal Command recorded repeated contacts as aircraft covered the threatened shipping.
episodes.outcome: Every merchant vessel in SC 130 survived this passage. The ships and aircraft shared responsibility for its defence.

episodes.title: From convoy protection to surrender patrols
episodes.action: As the war in Europe ended, Coastal Command crews patrolled to locate and follow U-boats complying with the surrender orders.
episodes.outcome: The May review documents air operations continuing through the handover. The convoys had carried the men and supplies needed for the Allied war in Europe.

name: Arctic convoys to the Soviet Union
question: Why did the experiences of PQ 17 and PQ 18 differ?
objective: The northern route delivered Allied supplies to Soviet ports. Merchant crews sailed within range of German aircraft based in occupied Norway.
turningPoint: The dispersal of PQ 17 in July 1942 left its ships exposed. PQ 18 sailed in September with a stronger escort and its own fighter carrier.
consequence: Supply resumed despite further losses. The September fighting demonstrated both the value and the limits of escort-carrier aviation.
gap: The number sailing, the number proceeding after turn-backs and the number arriving are distinct. Carrier diary sorties cover individual days.

episodes.title: Dervish reaches the Soviet Union
episodes.action: The first Arctic supply convoy reached Arkhangelsk from Iceland, inaugurating regular maritime traffic to the Soviet ally.
episodes.outcome: The official-history table records seven ships sailed and seven arrived. Later movements encountered very different conditions.

figures.label: Ships arriving with Dervish
figures.scope: Eastbound convoy Dervish, all seven ships in the table

episodes.title: PQ 17 sails for the Soviet Arctic
episodes.action: Merchant ships and escorts left Iceland with matériel for the Soviet Union. German reconnaissance followed their passage into the northern seas.
episodes.outcome: The convoy entered the zone of German air and sea power before news of a possible surface sortie reached the Admiralty.

episodes.title: PQ 17 ordered to scatter
episodes.action: The Admiralty feared an attack by German heavy warships. After dispersal the merchantmen tried to reach safety individually or in small groups.
episodes.outcome: Bombers and submarines found isolated ships. Only eleven merchant ships ultimately reached Soviet ports.

figures.label: Merchant ships reaching Soviet ports
figures.scope: Survivors of PQ 17

episodes.title: Avenger flies fighters for PQ 18
episodes.action: The escort carrier flew Sea Hurricanes while German bombers attacked the convoy. The carrier diary records the fighter effort separately from the convoy losses.
episodes.outcome: German aircraft sank merchant ships despite the fighter cover. Avenger continued operating on the following day.

figures.label: Sea Hurricane sorties
figures.scope: HMS Avenger fighter operations for PQ 18 that day

episodes.title: Scharnhorst lost off North Cape
episodes.action: German reconnaissance had located the eastbound convoy JW 55B. Scharnhorst sailed to intercept it while British cruisers and a distant covering force protected the convoy.
episodes.outcome: The Royal Navy sank Scharnhorst in the surface battle. The convoy ledger records the merchant passage separately from the German warship loss.

figures.label: Merchant ships reaching port with JW 55B
figures.scope: Table A, JW 55B arrivals at Kola Inlet

episodes.title: Final eastbound convoy arrives
episodes.action: JW 67 arrived after the end of hostilities in Europe. The return convoy RA 67 reached the Clyde on 31 May.
episodes.outcome: The last movements complete the convoy tables in both directions. Counts in the tables exclude ships lost after arrival in port.

figures.label: Ships arriving with JW 67
figures.scope: Last eastbound convoy in Table A

name: RAF Bomber Command night offensive
question: What did successive night offensives achieve over German cities?
objective: Bomber Command moved from small early operations to sustained attacks on German industrial regions. Industry, housing and the people living near it experienced different effects.
turningPoint: The Ruhr, Hamburg and Berlin campaigns tested whether repeated bombing could cripple industry and break German resistance.
consequence: Hamburg suffered catastrophic destruction. Berlin continued functioning through the winter offensive, while operating losses weighed heavily on bomber crews.
gap: Bomb weight is a measure of effort. The Hamburg police estimate describes residential damage in one city.

episodes.title: Operation Millennium over Cologne
episodes.action: Bomber Command used operational and training units for a mass raid on the night of 30–31 May. Crews and aircraft from training establishments made the size of the force possible.
episodes.outcome: The raid devastated districts of Cologne and demonstrated that the command could concentrate a much larger force on a single night.

episodes.title: Opening night of the Battle of the Ruhr
episodes.action: RAF Bomber Command attacked Essen on the night of 5–6 March, opening months of concentrated attacks on the industrial region.
episodes.outcome: Essen became one of a series of Ruhr targets. Night crews returned as industry and transport were repaired or dispersed.

episodes.title: Operation Gomorrah begins
episodes.action: British night bombers and American daylight forces attacked Hamburg. Four RAF night attacks extended from 24–25 July to 2–3 August.
episodes.outcome: Fires swept residential districts. The Hamburg police assessment makes it possible to distinguish housing destruction from bombs delivered.

figures.label: British night raids in the series
figures.scope: Hamburg, RAF main series

figures.label: Bomb weight in the RAF series

figures.label: Living accommodation destroyed

episodes.title: Winter battle over Berlin
episodes.action: Bomber Command opened its main winter series against Berlin. Australian crews took part in the night offensive.
episodes.outcome: Losses mounted over the winter. The offensive ended in March 1944 without bringing about a German collapse.

figures.label: Lancasters in the force
figures.scope: Berlin raid in the RAF official history, first major November attack

figures.label: Mosquitoes in the force

episodes.title: Air attacks on Dresden
episodes.action: RAF Bomber Command attacked during the night of 13–14 February. US forces followed by day on 14 and 15 February. Residents and refugees faced the fires and the destruction of large parts of the city.
episodes.outcome: Dresden’s historical commission examined burial, recovery and population records. Its upper estimate covers deaths in the February attacks by both air forces.

figures.label: Commission upper estimate of deaths
figures.scope: Dresden historical commission, all February attacks together

episodes.title: Operation Manna food drops
episodes.action: Bomber Command Lancasters flew food to Dutch civilians facing famine. The agreed reception areas included Waalhaven, Ypenburg, Duindigt and Valkenburg. USAAF aircraft subsequently joined the relief effort in Operation Chowhound.
episodes.outcome: Deliveries from the air began before the German surrender and complemented relief arriving by land and water. Food dropped and food actually distributed to families were different stages of the relief effort.

figures.label: Agreed reception areas for the first drops
figures.scope: Four agreed areas, excluding the unplanned release near Haamstede

name: The Blitz against British cities
question: What changed when the Luftwaffe shifted its attacks to British cities?
objective: Attacks on London’s docks and on industrial cities spread the air war into homes, factories and rail districts.
turningPoint: As large daylight formations gave way to night attacks, different British cities faced concentrated raids separated by intervals of recovery.
consequence: Heavy losses of life and housing disrupted daily life. London and the provincial cities continued to function.
gap: Coventry’s attacking force cannot be used as the campaign-wide strength of the Luftwaffe or as a count of aircraft reaching the city.

episodes.title: London’s docks and East End attacked
episodes.action: German aircraft struck the docks by day and returned after dark. Fires and destruction extended into the residential East End.
episodes.outcome: The raid began a sustained assault on the capital and altered the demands on Fighter Command and civil defence.

episodes.title: Coventry raid, night of 14–15 November
episodes.action: A concentrated German night attack hit engineering works, public buildings and homes across Coventry.
episodes.outcome: Damage to utilities and transport made relief harder. Destroyed houses and the cathedral became enduring evidence of the raid.

figures.label: Bomber force described in the despatch
figures.scope: Attacking force at Coventry, described as nearly 500

figures.label: People killed in the Coventry raid
figures.scope: Later British GCHQ historical account of the city raid

episodes.title: Final major London raid of the main Blitz
episodes.action: On the night of 10–11 May German aircraft struck the capital heavily again. The chambers of the House of Commons were among the buildings destroyed.
episodes.outcome: The main Blitz ended that month. Civil defence and the recovery of damaged districts continued.

figures.label: Civilian deaths in London
figures.scope: London-wide toll, House of Lords Library

name: Cross-Channel fighter offensive and Channel Dash
question: Could Britain draw German fighters into battle over occupied France?
objective: Fighter Command carried the air battle across the Channel through sweeps and escorted daylight operations.
turningPoint: Small early sweeps developed into larger operations. The February 1942 passage of German warships exposed the limits of British interception.
consequence: The offensive tied fighter units to the Channel front. Individual sorties carried very different risks for fighters, escorts and naval strike crews.
gap: The complete loss of one naval flight describes the Channel Dash action alone.

episodes.title: First cross-Channel fighter sweep of the offensive
episodes.action: Fighter Command sent a sweep over northern France as weather allowed the first move in the new offensive.
episodes.outcome: The patrol inaugurated a new pattern of daylight operations over territory where British pilots who came down faced capture.

episodes.title: Circus No. 1
episodes.action: Blenheims accompanied by fighters attacked a target in the Guînes area. The British expected the escorted bombers to draw a German response.
episodes.outcome: The operation gave the Circus series its starting point. The size of an escort did not guarantee an engagement with German fighters.

figures.label: Blenheims at the rendezvous
figures.scope: No. 114 Squadron, first Circus operation

figures.label: Fighter squadrons at the rendezvous
figures.scope: Six named fighter squadrons in the RAF account, paragraph 43

episodes.title: The Channel Dash
episodes.action: German warships Scharnhorst, Gneisenau and Prinz Eugen passed through the Channel with air cover. Naval aviators from Manston joined the British response.
episodes.outcome: All six Swordfish of 825 Naval Air Squadron were lost. Five of their eighteen aircrew survived and the ships reached German waters.

figures.label: Swordfish lost
figures.scope: 825 Naval Air Squadron strike flight

figures.label: Aircrew who survived
figures.scope: 18 aircrew of the six Swordfish

episodes.title: Mitchell units join the escorted daylight offensive
episodes.action: By mid-May the Mitchell force joined No. 2 Group’s Boston and Ventura squadrons in daylight operations. The RAF history distinguishes the fighter-offensive purpose of Circus from the bombing priority in Ramrod operations.
episodes.outcome: The change widened the range of aircraft used over occupied Europe shortly before No. 2 Group transferred to the tactical air force.

name: V-weapons, Crossbow and Operation Diver
question: How did the air war against the V-weapons change after the launches began?
objective: The Allies attacked the German weapons programme before launches began and later mounted a separate defence of cities under attack.
turningPoint: The V-1 offensive against Britain in June 1944 added a sustained air-defence task. After the advance across France, Antwerp became a major target.
consequence: British defences intercepted flying bombs. V-2 impacts still caused heavy casualties in liberated Europe, including at the Rex cinema.
gap: Bombing effort, intercepted V-1s and deaths from one V-2 count different outcomes. The Antwerp observation covers a single impact.

episodes.title: Peenemünde attacked, night of 17–18 August
episodes.action: RAF Bomber Command attacked the German research establishment. People in the labour camp and nearby housing were among the victims.
episodes.outcome: The raid interrupted work and contributed to dispersal. German development and subsequent launches continued.

episodes.title: First V-1 strikes against Britain
episodes.action: Flying bombs reached England after the Normandy landings. Operation Diver brought fighters and ground-based defences into the defence of south-east England.
episodes.outcome: Interceptions reduced the number reaching London. The civilian population remained exposed to impacts and falling debris.

figures.label: V-1 flying bombs launched
figures.scope: First phase in the Historic England report, rounded figure

figures.label: V-1 flying bombs reaching London
figures.scope: London arrivals in the same first phase

episodes.title: V-2 strikes a crowded Antwerp cinema
episodes.action: A rocket struck the Rex during a film screening. The municipal account distinguishes service personnel from civilians in the audience.
episodes.outcome: The Antwerp record gives 567 deaths. The two categories below belong to that same total.

figures.label: People killed at the Cinema Rex

name: Scheldt estuary and Walcheren
question: Why did the liberation of Antwerp leave its port unusable?
objective: The Allies held the port but German troops controlled the estuary. Ships could reach Antwerp only after the approaches were cleared.
turningPoint: British bombing breached Walcheren’s sea defences. Inundation altered the ground battle and displaced island residents.
consequence: The landings, surrender of the defenders and subsequent minesweeping opened the estuary. Water remained in villages long after the battle.
gap: The Westkapelle memorial count covers a series of attacks. The first convoy arrived weeks after the island landings.

episodes.title: Warnings dropped over Walcheren
episodes.action: Aircraft dropped notices asking inhabitants to leave areas threatened by inundation. Many people had little opportunity to reach safety.
episodes.outcome: The warnings preceded the breach at Westkapelle by one day.

figures.label: Aircraft distributing warnings
figures.scope: Leaflet operation over Walcheren

episodes.title: Bombing breaches the sea dyke
episodes.action: Bombers attacked the dyke beside Westkapelle. Water entered the island and later attacks widened or added breaches.
episodes.outcome: The village sustained a heavy civilian death toll across the October attacks. Flooding also restricted movements of both armies.

figures.label: Villagers killed across the attacks
figures.scope: Westkapelle local memorial, cumulative village toll

episodes.title: Landings on Walcheren
episodes.action: Allied troops landed on the island while other forces crossed from the mainland. Flooded terrain shaped the final fighting.
episodes.outcome: The defenders were overcome. Minesweepers still had to clear the shipping channel before Antwerp could receive convoys.

figures.label: First Canadian Army casualties
figures.scope: Multinational First Canadian Army, killed, wounded and missing

figures.label: Canadian casualties
figures.scope: Canadian subset of the First Canadian Army casualties

episodes.title: First seagoing convoy reaches Antwerp
episodes.action: Merchant ships sailed up the cleared Scheldt after the estuary battle and minesweeping.
episodes.outcome: The port began receiving supplies for the advance into Germany. This was the operational result of weeks of combined operations.

name: Ardennes and the Bastogne airlift
question: What difference did the break in the weather make to Bastogne?
objective: The German counteroffensive began in weather that limited Allied air reconnaissance and support. Encirclement left Bastogne short of essential supplies.
turningPoint: A clearer sky on 23 December allowed troop carriers to reach the garrison as tactical aircraft returned over the battlefield.
consequence: Air supply helped sustain the defenders until ground forces reopened a road. Allied air attacks also complicated German movement.
gap: Bundles, tons and aircraft measure the same resupply from different perspectives. Supplies dropped can differ from supplies recovered.

episodes.title: German winter offensive begins
episodes.action: German armies attacked through poor flying weather. Allied aircraft had limited opportunity to observe and intervene during the opening advance.
episodes.outcome: American positions were overrun or bypassed and Bastogne became an isolated road junction.

episodes.title: Weather holds back the transport aircraft
episodes.action: The garrison needed ammunition and medical stores. Efforts to get supplies in by air were frustrated by conditions.
episodes.outcome: Defenders waited another day for large-scale resupply while the encirclement continued.

episodes.title: Troop carriers resupply Bastogne
episodes.action: Transport aircraft flew over the perimeter and released bundles for the encircled garrison. The US Army reconstruction gives separate aircraft, bundle and tonnage totals.
episodes.outcome: The drop relieved immediate shortages. American ground troops reached the perimeter on 26 December.

figures.scope: Bastogne perimeter, source unit retained

name: Rhineland, Remagen and Rhine crossings
question: How did air operations support the crossing of the Rhine?
objective: Allied armies needed to reach the Rhine, secure crossings and bring formations and stores to the far bank.
turningPoint: The bridge at Remagen offered an unexpected crossing. Farther north, an airborne operation accompanied the deliberate crossing at Wesel.
consequence: The bridgeheads endured. Airborne troops joined the ground advance east of the Rhine after suffering losses on the landing grounds.
gap: Airborne strength covers Varsity’s lift. It excludes troops crossing by boat and cannot measure the whole Rhineland campaign.

episodes.title: Operation Clarion opens
episodes.action: Allied air forces attacked transport facilities across a broad area as armies prepared to advance through the Rhineland.
episodes.outcome: Damage and disruption were spread across many towns. Individual yards and routes recovered at different rates.

episodes.title: Bridge captured at Remagen
episodes.action: American troops seized the Ludendorff Bridge. German efforts from the air formed part of the attempt to eliminate the crossing.
episodes.outcome: The bridgehead survived. Ground engineers added crossings as the original structure deteriorated.

episodes.title: Operation Varsity follows the Plunder crossing
episodes.action: British and American airborne divisions landed east of the river while troops crossing the Rhine advanced toward them.
episodes.outcome: The airborne troops secured key ground and linked with the river crossing. The landing brought concentrated losses to troops and transport crews.

figures.label: Airborne divisions landed
figures.scope: British 6th and US 17th in Varsity

figures.label: Airborne troops involved
figures.scope: Museum account of Varsity, over 16,000

name: Yugoslavia, Greece and the Balkan air war
question: How did Allied aviation return to the Balkans after the 1941 defeat?
objective: Axis air power accompanied the invasion of Yugoslavia and Greece. After the Allied withdrawal, air support and liaison with local resistance increasingly depended on flights from outside the occupied countries.
turningPoint: Bases in Italy later made regular supply and evacuation possible. The Balkan Air Force worked alongside Yugoslav partisans and other Allied organisations.
consequence: Aircraft connected isolated fighting forces and carried thousands of wounded people out. Different monthly reporting series cover different countries.
gap: The 1944 evacuation table covers Yugoslavia and Greece. The January–April 1945 table covers Yugoslavia and Albania. Neither is a total for every partisan flight.

episodes.title: Invasion of Yugoslavia and Greece
episodes.action: German air attacks on Belgrade opened alongside the ground invasion. Allied air forces in Greece faced pressure on their airfields and the withdrawing armies.
episodes.outcome: The collapse in Yugoslavia exposed the Allied flank in Greece and forced successive withdrawals.

episodes.title: Allied evacuation from Greece
episodes.action: British and Commonwealth forces embarked from southern Greek ports. Air attacks made daylight movement and embarkation dangerous.
episodes.outcome: Many troops reached Crete or Egypt. The evacuation cost transport, equipment and lives and left Crete exposed.

episodes.title: Operation Ratweek
episodes.action: The Balkan Air Force opened a coordinated campaign with Tito’s partisans against the communications used by German forces withdrawing from the southern Balkans.
episodes.outcome: Air attack and partisan action disrupted routes during the withdrawal. Their separate contributions cannot be isolated from the combined operation.

figures.label: Balkan Air Force sorties during September
figures.scope: Entire Balkan Air Force monthly activity, wider than Ratweek alone

episodes.title: Four months of Balkan air evacuation
episodes.action: From August through November Allied special operations aircraft carried people out on flights that also served the resistance. The Mediterranean Allied Air Forces kept monthly landing and passenger returns.
episodes.outcome: The table records thousands of wounded evacuees and other passengers. Its October entries include operations connected with the British occupation of Greece.

episodes.title: Last spring evacuation return
episodes.action: The separate 1945 return counted flights to Yugoslavia and Albania. April recorded many more wounded passengers than the preceding months.
episodes.outcome: The transport network was still evacuating casualties in the final weeks of the war in Europe.

name: Battle of Crete and Operation Mercury
question: Why did the battle turn on Maleme airfield?
objective: German airborne forces needed a foothold on Crete. Greek and Commonwealth defenders contested the airfields while the Royal Navy opposed reinforcement by sea.
turningPoint: Maleme came under German control by the night of 21 May, allowing reinforcements to land. Fighting elsewhere on the island continued.
consequence: Allied troops retreated across the island to evacuation ports. German airborne troops suffered severe casualties despite the capture of Crete.
gap: The opening-day landing figure and the Sphakia evacuation cover different forces, directions and dates.

episodes.title: Operation Mercury opens
episodes.action: German airborne troops landed near the island’s airfields and met resistance from New Zealand, Australian, British and Greek defenders.
episodes.outcome: The attackers suffered severe losses. The three principal airfields did not all change hands together.

figures.label: Airborne troops landed on the first day

episodes.title: Maleme opens to reinforcements
episodes.action: After the New Zealand withdrawal from ground overlooking Maleme, German troops secured the airfield. Transport aircraft brought in additional forces.
episodes.outcome: The German foothold in western Crete expanded while defenders elsewhere still held their positions.

episodes.title: Evacuation from the south coast
episodes.action: Troops crossed the mountains to Sphakia on foot. Royal Navy vessels embarked men over four nights while other forces evacuated or surrendered elsewhere.
episodes.outcome: More than twelve thousand were taken off from Sphakia. Others remained behind and became prisoners, while some escaped with Cretan help.

name: Operation Dragoon and southern France
question: What did the airborne landing contribute to the invasion of Provence?
objective: The Mediterranean Allies wanted a second entry into France and access to the southern ports. Airborne troops were to hold the approaches inland from the beaches.
turningPoint: Parachutists landed through fog on 15 August. Later glider lifts added men and heavier equipment to the inland lodgement.
consequence: The landings succeeded and French forces liberated the ports. Marseille and Toulon became supply gateways for the Allied advance.
gap: The museum’s parachutist figure counts Americans. British and glider-borne participants belong to different populations.

episodes.title: Parachute landings inland from the beaches
episodes.action: The multinational First Airborne Task Force landed before the seaborne assault. Fog scattered some drops around Le Muy.
episodes.outcome: Airborne troops assembled inland and contested approaches to the beachhead while the assault forces came ashore.

figures.label: American parachutists
figures.scope: US parachutists in the museum account, excludes glider troops and British parachutists

episodes.title: Bluebird and Dove glider lifts
episodes.action: Gliders reinforced the parachute landing later that day, bringing troops and equipment. The American 550th Glider Infantry Battalion took part.
episodes.outcome: The lifts strengthened the inland force despite poor landing conditions and damaged gliders.

episodes.title: Southern ports secured
episodes.action: French troops overcame German resistance at Marseille and Toulon as other Allied units pursued the retreat north.
episodes.outcome: The Allies gained two major ports. Damage and mines still had to be cleared before their capacity could be realised.

name: Western Desert, El Alamein, Torch and Tunisia
question: How did the desert air war become a campaign fought from both ends of North Africa?
objective: Aircraft protected armies and ports along the narrow coastal supply routes. Changing front lines repeatedly placed airfields beyond the reach of maintenance and fuel.
turningPoint: The desert offensive at El Alamein coincided with the Allied landings far to the west. Axis forces fell back on Tunisia and increasingly depended on reinforcement across the Mediterranean.
consequence: Air, ground and naval forces converged on Tunisia. The Axis surrender ended the North African fighting and opened a route toward Sicily.
gap: A squadron’s flight structure is a formation snapshot. Air-bridge losses, aircraft available and the eventual scale of the surrender are separate measures.

episodes.title: No. 3 Squadron RAAF arrives in Egypt
episodes.action: The Australian squadron arrived without its aircraft and came under RAF Middle East Command. It was organised for army cooperation, with fighter and reconnaissance elements.
episodes.outcome: The unit joined the first Libyan campaign, which included Operation Compass, and later returned for the fighting in the Western Desert.

figures.label: Flights in the squadron’s initial organisation
figures.scope: No. 3 Squadron RAAF in Egypt, organisational elements

figures.label: Flights equipped with fighters
figures.scope: Two of the three flights, Gladiator and Gauntlet fighters

episodes.title: Tobruk isolated
episodes.action: Axis forces advanced east while the port held out. The RAF and the Royal Navy supported a garrison increasingly dependent on its maritime connection.
episodes.outcome: Holding the port denied its facilities to the Axis and imposed a continuing air and sea supply burden on the Allies.

episodes.title: Second Battle of El Alamein begins
episodes.action: The Desert Air Force supported the Eighth Army as it attacked in Egypt. The battle grew out of months of air fighting over the desert supply routes.
episodes.outcome: The breakthrough forced the Axis retreat west and required Allied squadrons to move forward behind the army.

episodes.place: Algiers and the western landing areas
episodes.title: Operation Torch opens a western front
episodes.action: Allied forces landed in French Morocco and Algeria. Carriers and newly occupied airfields supported operations at widely separated ports.
episodes.outcome: Allied columns approached Tunisia from the west, while Axis aircraft and shipping carried reinforcements into the bridgehead.

episodes.place: Strait of Sicily, approaches to Tunisia
episodes.title: Operation Flax and the Tunisian air bridge
episodes.action: Allied fighters intercepted Axis transports crossing toward or returning from Tunisia. These flights were part of the wider effort to sustain the bridgehead.
episodes.outcome: Transport losses restricted an increasingly precarious supply route. Aircrew claims and German transport losses require separate returns.

figures.label: Ju 52 transports destroyed
figures.scope: German air transport losses in the Operation Flax account, wider than the 18 April engagement

figures.label: Ju 52 transports damaged
figures.scope: German air transport losses in the Operation Flax account, wider than the 18 April engagement

figures.label: Me 323 transports lost
figures.scope: German air transport losses in the Operation Flax account, wider than the 18 April engagement

episodes.title: Axis resistance ends in Tunisia
episodes.action: Converging Allied forces captured the remaining Axis positions. The desert and Tunisian air forces could turn to the central Mediterranean.
episodes.outcome: Surrender ended the North African campaign, bringing Sicily within reach from Allied bases.

name: Siege of Leningrad and the Ladoga airlift
question: What could aircraft carry into a city cut off by land?
objective: The siege isolated Leningrad from its normal supply routes. Aircraft carried high-priority food and ammunition in and evacuated people on return flights, alongside a much larger Ladoga transport effort.
turningPoint: The autumn 1941 transport returns record both directions of flight. In January 1943 a narrow land corridor changed the supply situation.
consequence: A year later the siege was lifted. Air transport had relieved some shortages and taken civilians to safety, while hunger killed on a scale the airlift could not prevent.
gap: The transport organisations and the city evacuation commission used different time windows and registers. Food is included in cargo totals.

episodes.title: Start of the autumn airlift reporting period
episodes.action: Soviet civil and military transport crews flew priority supplies into the besieged city and carried people and industrial items east on return flights.
episodes.outcome: Archived returns count flights, inbound cargo and outbound passengers separately. The reporting window here ends on 31 December.

episodes.title: Air raids on the Baltic Fleet at Kronstadt
episodes.action: German bombers attacked warships in and around Kronstadt over several days. Soviet shipboard and shore-based guns contested the attacks. Marat sustained catastrophic damage.
episodes.outcome: The damaged battleship settled in shallow water. Some of its guns remained available for the defence of Leningrad, qualifying the German description of the ship as sunk.

episodes.place: Shlisselburg, south shore of Lake Ladoga
episodes.title: Operation Iskra opens a corridor
episodes.action: The Leningrad and Volkhov fronts broke through south of Lake Ladoga. The corridor restored a narrow land connection to the city.
episodes.outcome: A railway could be built through the corridor, changing the burden on the lake and air routes even while the siege continued.

episodes.title: Siege lifted
episodes.action: A Soviet offensive drove German forces far enough from Leningrad to end the siege. The city marked its liberation on 27 January.
episodes.outcome: The immediate siege ended after more than two years. Much of the city's population and infrastructure had already been lost.

name: Finland, the Winter War and Continuation War
question: How did the air war over Finland change between the two wars?
objective: In the Winter War a small Finnish air force defended cities and supported troops against a much larger Soviet force. Hostilities resumed in June 1941 under different strategic circumstances.
turningPoint: Soviet long-range aviation attacked Helsinki on three nights in February 1944. The summer offensive brought the air battle back to the Karelian Isthmus.
consequence: Finland left the war against the Soviet Union in September 1944. The municipal damage record and Soviet operations over the front describe distinct parts of the campaign.
gap: The wars were separated by the 1940–41 interim peace. February totals combine three Helsinki raids, and the inner-city count is part of the wider city total.

episodes.title: Winter War opens with attacks on Finnish cities
episodes.action: Soviet aviation attacked Helsinki as Soviet ground forces crossed the frontier. Finnish fighters and anti-aircraft units contested raids throughout the winter.
episodes.outcome: The March 1940 peace ended this phase. Finland continued building its air arm during the interval before the next war.

episodes.title: Air attacks and the opening of the Continuation War
episodes.action: Soviet aircraft attacked targets in Finland days after Germany invaded the Soviet Union. Finland entered a second war against the Soviet Union.
episodes.outcome: The air and ground fronts reopened after the interim peace. Finnish and German forces now operated against a common enemy.

episodes.title: Three nights of bombing against Helsinki
episodes.action: Soviet long-range aviation attacked on 6–7, 16–17 and 26–27 February. Finland’s 1st Anti-Aircraft Regiment defended the capital.
episodes.outcome: Helsinki’s historical account distinguishes bombs dropped across the operation from impacts inside the city and in its central districts.

episodes.title: Soviet summer offensive on the isthmus
episodes.action: Soviet forces opened their offensive against Finnish positions. Weather affected the planned participation of long-range aviation near Viipuri.
episodes.outcome: The advance forced Finnish units back. Operational plans, aborts and actual arrivals over a target describe different levels of effort.

episodes.title: Armistice with the Soviet Union
episodes.action: After the September ceasefire Finland signed the Moscow Armistice. This ended the Continuation War and required the removal of German forces.
episodes.outcome: The northern fighting that followed against Germany was a separate war, with a different opponent.

name: Crimea, the Caucasus and the Kuban bridgehead
question: Why did the air war repeatedly return to the Kerch Strait?
objective: The strait connected Crimea with the Taman peninsula. Sevastopol, the Caucasus advance and the Kuban bridgehead each put different demands on air and sea transport.
turningPoint: The German retreat from the Caucasus left an army dependent on a bridgehead. The Luftwaffe diverted transport and rescue aircraft to its supply.
consequence: The Axis evacuated Taman in October 1943. Soviet forces subsequently recovered Crimea, including Sevastopol, in May 1944.
gap: The flying-boat allocation describes one element of the transport effort. It cannot be treated as the entire airlift or as the strength of the opposing air armies.

episodes.title: Second Axis assault on Sevastopol
episodes.action: German IV Air Corps returned to support the December assault on the fortress. The campaign history identifies separate bomber, dive-bomber and fighter allocations.
episodes.outcome: The attack failed to secure Sevastopol, and IV Air Corps moved away. The forces committed here preceded the much larger June 1942 assault.

episodes.title: Final Axis ground assault on Sevastopol
episodes.action: German and Romanian forces attacked the Soviet fortress after an air and artillery bombardment. Soviet defenders and the Black Sea Fleet struggled to keep the garrison supplied.
episodes.outcome: The last defences collapsed in early July. The same port would change hands again less than two years later.

episodes.title: Supplying the Kuban bridgehead
episodes.action: As the German Seventeenth Army withdrew from the Caucasus, aircraft supplemented the limited crossing capacity. Air-sea rescue flying boats joined the transport effort.
episodes.outcome: The bridgehead held through the spring. Diverting specialised aircraft illustrates the cost of sustaining it in winter.

episodes.title: Air fighting above the Soviet beachhead
episodes.action: German aircraft supported the attempt to eliminate the Soviet foothold at Myskhako. Soviet aviation contested the airspace over a narrow coastal front.
episodes.outcome: The beachhead survived. Air fighting continued across the Kuban as Soviet forces pressed toward Krymskaya.

episodes.title: Axis evacuation of Taman completed
episodes.action: Axis troops crossed into Crimea after a staged withdrawal from the bridgehead. Soviet forces recovered the peninsula.
episodes.outcome: The Kerch Strait became the front line again, with air and sea movement central to the next campaign.

episodes.title: Soviet troops retake Sevastopol
episodes.action: The Soviet advance through Crimea reached Sevastopol as Axis forces attempted to evacuate by sea and air.
episodes.outcome: The city fell on 9 May and the remaining Axis positions in Crimea collapsed in the following days.

name: Ukraine after Kursk, the Dnieper and Korsun
question: What could airborne troops and air transport contribute after Kursk?
objective: The Red Army sought bridgeheads across the Dnieper during its advance into Ukraine. Aircraft carried parachute troops across the river and later supported very different fighting around Korsun.
turningPoint: The September drop scattered Soviet formations. Survivors regrouped and later fought alongside ground forces. The German pocket at Korsun created an air-supply emergency the following winter.
consequence: Kyiv returned to Soviet control and the German front retreated. At Korsun aircraft sustained a pocket temporarily before its surviving troops broke out.
gap: The regrouped airborne strength is an October estimate. It is smaller in scope than the original lift and says nothing about total German air transport losses at Korsun.

episodes.title: Airborne landing west of the Dnieper
episodes.action: Soviet troops jumped on the night of 24–25 September. Scattered drops and communications failures made it difficult to assemble the planned force.
episodes.outcome: Survivors joined local partisans and formed a composite brigade. Its October strength is a later observation than the initial landings.

figures.label: Strength of the regrouped brigade
figures.scope: Composite brigade at the end of October, reported at up to 1,200 including partisans

episodes.title: Kyiv recaptured
episodes.action: Soviet armies advanced from bridgeheads north of Kyiv. Fighting at other crossings continued after the city fell.
episodes.outcome: The Dnieper line was breached. Farther downstream regrouped parachutists later supported the 52nd Army’s crossing operations.

episodes.title: Korsun pocket closes
episodes.action: The encirclement isolated German formations. Luftwaffe transports carried supplies into the pocket and took wounded men out when landing was possible.
episodes.outcome: Deteriorating conditions reduced the value of the airstrip. Surviving troops attempted a ground breakout in mid-February.

episodes.title: Supplies landed and dropped at Korsun
episodes.action: Initial reports distinguished aircraft landing stores at the airfield from containers dropped to the garrison. The amounts landed were reported in separate units for ammunition and fuel.
episodes.outcome: The day brought a temporary improvement in air supply. The initial return could not establish how many of the dropped containers ground troops recovered.

name: Romania, Ploiești and the August reversal
question: Did attacks on Ploiești permanently remove Romanian oil from Axis supply?
objective: Romanian oil mattered to the Axis and placed the refineries at Ploiești high on the Allied target list. Romania’s air force initially helped defend the country alongside Germany.
turningPoint: A costly American attack in 1943 was followed by a sustained 1944 offensive. A Soviet ground breakthrough and Romania’s August change of sides then transformed the situation.
consequence: Bombing interrupted refining to varying degrees. Loss of access to Romanian oil and the reversal of Romanian military alignment went beyond the effects of any individual raid.
gap: Tidal Wave’s losses belong to one mission. A change of allegiance in August requires Romanian forces to be identified by date.

episodes.title: Early American raid on the oil region
episodes.action: American heavy bombers operating from the Middle East attacked the Romanian oil area, an early demonstration of the distance involved.
episodes.outcome: The limited raid preceded the much larger operations mounted from North Africa and Italy.

episodes.title: Operation Tidal Wave
episodes.action: American B-24 groups flew from Libya against the refineries. Romanian and German defences inflicted severe losses.
episodes.outcome: Damage interrupted production but repairs restored much of the capacity. The USAF museum records 54 bombers that failed to return from a force of 178.

episodes.title: Final Fifteenth Air Force raid on Ploiești
episodes.action: American bombers struck the refinery area for the final time as Soviet forces prepared their offensive in Romania.
episodes.outcome: The air campaign ended days before the Romanian government changed sides. It had involved repeated attacks from Italian bases.

episodes.title: Romania changes sides
episodes.action: King Michael removed Antonescu as Soviet forces broke through in the Iași–Chișinău offensive. German forces attempted to overturn the change, including attacks on Bucharest.
episodes.outcome: Romanian pilots fought former German allies. Their later operations over Hungary belong to a different coalition from their defence of the oil region.

name: Hungary, Budapest and Lake Balaton
question: Could the isolated Budapest garrison be supplied by air through the winter?
objective: The Debrecen and Budapest offensives brought Soviet, Romanian, German and Hungarian aviation over a rapidly moving front. Encirclement made supply flights essential to the Budapest defenders.
turningPoint: Air transport continued through bad weather and Soviet opposition. A German retrospective return and a second account give substantially different totals.
consequence: The capital fell in February. Fighting shifted to Lake Balaton, where the German March offensive failed to reverse the Soviet advance.
gap: The two airlift figures are competing estimates for the same interval. Some dropped supplies never reached the defenders.

episodes.title: Debrecen offensive begins
episodes.action: The Soviet advance into Hungary brought major air fighting above mobile ground forces. German and Hungarian formations opposed the advance, while Romania now fought on the Soviet side.
episodes.outcome: The campaign moved toward Budapest after the Debrecen operation ended in late October.

episodes.title: Encirclement of Budapest
episodes.action: The city was cut off and the German and Hungarian defenders depended on an airlift. The Budapest supply staff recorded deliveries while ground fighting consumed much of the city.
episodes.outcome: A 25 February German return and an alternative figure quoted in the Hungarian study disagree on the tonnage. Neither measures what individual units recovered.

figures.label: Military supplies in the OKL return
figures.scope: 25 February German return, Versorgungsstab Budapest

figures.label: Alternative total quoted by the study
figures.scope: Alternative for the same airlift, non-additive

episodes.title: Resistance in Budapest ends
episodes.action: The last organised Axis resistance in the capital collapsed after a failed breakout. Supplies dropped in the later phases had often fallen outside defenders’ control.
episodes.outcome: The Soviet forces could shift their effort west. The airlift had failed to secure the garrison’s survival.

episodes.title: Lake Balaton offensive opens
episodes.action: Germany mounted its final major offensive in Hungary. Soviet and Axis aircraft supported the ground battle in difficult early-spring conditions.
episodes.outcome: The German attack stalled and the Soviet advance resumed. The Balaton defensive operation ran through 15 March.

name: Baltic states, Tallinn and Courland
question: How did the Baltic air war change as the ground front moved toward the coast?
objective: Long-range aircraft struck Tallinn while it remained under German occupation. Later the fighting shifted to withdrawal routes and the sea supply of German forces isolated in Courland.
turningPoint: The evacuation of Estonia in September and the severing of the land route to Courland in October increased the importance of shipping.
consequence: The Tallinn raid devastated civilian areas. Army Group Courland retained contact by sea until the final German surrender.
gap: The Soviet flying return counts flights and completed missions separately. Shipping casualties during evacuation and the later Courland supply traffic belong to different operations.

episodes.title: Soviet night raid on Tallinn
episodes.action: Soviet long-range aviation attacked in two waves on 9–10 March. Researchers compared its headquarters returns with damage recorded in the city.
episodes.outcome: Residential neighbourhoods and cultural buildings burned. The flying return separates all flights from those credited with accomplishing the mission.

episodes.place: Tallinn and Gulf of Riga evacuation routes
episodes.title: Withdrawal from Tallinn and loss of Moero
episodes.action: German troops evacuated Estonia as Soviet forces entered Tallinn. The German naval diary records the loss of the evacuation ship Moero in a Soviet air attack at sea.
episodes.outcome: The evacuation moved troops, wounded people and civilians. The naval diary documents a separate maritime loss during the retreat.

episodes.title: Army Group North cut off in Courland
episodes.action: Soviet forces reached the Baltic, separating the German forces in Latvia from East Prussia. Shipping became the main connection with German-held ports.
episodes.outcome: German formations remained in Courland over the winter. Air and naval operations continued along the routes that sustained them.

episodes.title: Surrender in Courland
episodes.action: With Germany’s capitulation the isolated army group surrendered in Latvia. The ports had remained essential throughout months of fighting.
episodes.outcome: The surrender closed the Courland campaign. Movements of soldiers and refugees by sea had continued into the final days.

name: Vistula–Oder offensive and the Warsaw advance
question: How much could Soviet aviation fly during the opening breakthrough?
objective: Soviet armies concentrated in the Vistula bridgeheads for a westward advance into Poland and Germany. Winter weather limited the air support available at the outset.
turningPoint: The 16th Air Army recorded limited flying in the first two days of the 1st Belorussian Front’s attack. Improving visibility enabled reconnaissance to follow the German retreat.
consequence: Warsaw fell and Soviet troops reached the Oder. The rapid displacement of the front made forward airfields and their supply increasingly important.
gap: The two-day sortie total belongs to one air army on one front. The 1st Ukrainian Front opened its own offensive two days earlier.

episodes.title: 1st Ukrainian Front leaves the Vistula bridgehead
episodes.action: Konev’s front attacked from the Sandomierz area, opening the southern arm of the offensive in winter conditions.
episodes.outcome: The ground advance developed rapidly, before the opening of the corresponding offensive farther north.

episodes.title: 1st Belorussian Front attacks
episodes.action: Zhukov’s front attacked from the central Vistula bridgeheads. Poor weather restricted the 16th Air Army to a limited number of sorties in the first two days.
episodes.outcome: On 16 January reconnaissance could identify retreating columns and routes. The two-day return documents how little of the air army’s potential had initially been available.

figures.label: Sorties by the 16th Air Army
figures.scope: 1st Belorussian Front, first two days of its offensive

episodes.title: Warsaw taken
episodes.action: Polish and Soviet troops entered Warsaw as German units withdrew. Soviet aviation increasingly operated against columns west of the city.
episodes.outcome: The city lay in ruins after the occupation and 1944 uprising. The westward offensive continued toward Poznań and the Oder.

episodes.title: Advance reaches the Oder
episodes.action: Forward troops of the 1st Belorussian Front reached the Oder and established bridgeheads north of Küstrin. Air units were still moving forward across Poland.
episodes.outcome: The river became the next operational boundary. Fighting for the bridgeheads continued before the April attack on Berlin.

name: East Prussia, Königsberg and Pillau
question: What can the records establish about the air attack during the fall of Königsberg?
objective: The Soviet offensive isolated German centres of resistance in East Prussia. Civilians fled toward coastal evacuation routes as the land front contracted.
turningPoint: The April assault concentrated several Soviet air formations over Königsberg. Even historical studies that agree on the bomber force give different fighter-escort counts.
consequence: The city capitulated on 9 April. Fighting for Pillau and the coastal evacuation routes continued after the surrender of Königsberg.
gap: The two escort counts describe the same 7 April attack. They are alternatives and cannot be summed or turned into a confirmed loss figure.

episodes.title: East Prussian offensive opens
episodes.action: The 3rd Belorussian Front began its attack toward Königsberg. Snow and poor visibility limited flying during early stages.
episodes.outcome: The ground advance isolated German pockets and drove refugees toward the Baltic coast.

episodes.title: 18th Air Army attacks during the assault
episodes.action: The Soviet long-range force flew a rare mass daylight operation during the ground assault that had begun on 6 April. Baltic Fleet aviation and other air armies also took part in the wider battle.
episodes.outcome: Two studies give the same number of bombers for this attack and different escort strengths. The city’s capitulation followed on 9 April.

episodes.title: Königsberg garrison capitulates
episodes.action: The German garrison surrendered after the combined Soviet air, artillery and ground assault. Civilian survivors faced displacement and loss of homes.
episodes.outcome: The fall of the city left the remaining German forces concentrated on the coast.

episodes.title: Pillau falls
episodes.action: Soviet troops reached the Baltic port after fighting on the Samland peninsula. German sea evacuations had carried soldiers and civilians away while the route remained open.
episodes.outcome: The capture of Pillau closed a major East Prussian port during the final weeks of the European war.
